utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just please look at the heading just above that on the left-hand corner at the top. Does that say Medicinski Centre Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't really see very clearly because it's not a good copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, can you please turn to the third document which is in that bundle there. Is that a certificate from the Dubrovnik Neretva district -- medical centre Dubrovnik of the 13th of December, 1994, referring to your injuries and your duties?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is from the Dubrovnik medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours like that read onto the record for the moment perhaps by the translators who have a copy of it in the interpretation booth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend and colleague marked this document with the wrong date, I believe, because at the bottom of the document you can see the 13th of March, 1995, not the 13th of December, 1992, as has been mistakenly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Are you content with that correction, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I'd be grateful, indeed, if the interpreters would be able to read that document from the copy they have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Medical history, the 6th of December, 1991. Wounded by a shell, sustained number of different injuries to the head, chest, and legs. Shrapnel lodged in the right leg, lung, neck. Since then tauper [as interpreted] in the head, headache, pressure, pain in the chest. Has become oversensitive, often nervous, numb in one-half of the head, extending to stomach, has a feeling of weight and contraction. Once Ladiomil medicine is administered, he feels relieved. Lack of sleep, wakes up often, is visited by thoughts, in a foul mood, worried. Psycho-motorically unobtrusive, tense, anxious, dysphoric, mostly depressed, exogenous cause. Neurologically, signs D and V, th:Praxiten 15, 3x1," illegible, "o, 00," illegible, "Cerson one pill, as necessary, DBK 13 March, presumably 1995." Signature missing at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the interpreter for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the interpreter also read onto the record the discharge papers of the 12th of December, 1991. That's the one-page document headed "Medical centre Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Letter of discharge. Mato Valjalo, born in Dubrovnik in 1943, was treated at this ward from the 6th of December to the 12th of December, 1991. He was wounded on the 6th of December, 1991. He sustained several explosive wounds of which the largest is in the neck area and is 4 centimetres in size and also has an entry-exit wound in the area of the medial side of the right thigh. The wounds were dealt with. The patient was hospitalised and was administered," illegible and illegible, "protection. The wounds are dressed daily. They are healing normally without infection." And then there's a diagnosis in Latin. "On the 12th of December, 1991, the patient was released with a recommendation for further treatment and rehabilitation outside Dubrovnik. "Chief of service, Dr. Stjepan Bogdanovic, medical doctor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you once again for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, I just want to ask you about the second document there, the one which is from the medical centre of Dubrovnik and is only of one page and appears to have been cut off. Mr. Valjalo, can you please pick up the documents. It's the one immediately in front of you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where the second page of that document is?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why, but this document is correct, because I didn't feel well and I went to see these doctors. So it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, what I'm asking you is: Are you in a position, if the document is at your home, to provide it to the Prosecution, and we can give it to the Trial Chamber at a later point, any missing pages?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to find all this when I get home to Dubrovnik, and I'll send it to you. I think I will be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May these three documents be tendered into evidence? And in offering them into evidence, the Prosecution puts on the record that we provided these three documents to Defence counsel this morning before court, and they were in a position to know the true position of the discharge letters and so on while the cross-examination continued this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The three documents will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic -- sorry, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Your Honour, it's correct that our learned friend Mr. Re disclosed these documents to us, but this was just before the Trial Chamber entered the courtroom, and we have not had an opportunity to study these documents in detail because we started our cross-examination right away. That's one point. My second point concerns the Defence objection to this document with the second page missing and without any date or doctor's signature or stamp. That is why we object to this document. If at a later date this document is delivered, the Defence will not object. After these documents are given exhibit numbers, I ask your leave to address you with reference to some of the other documents in the set disclosed to us today which the Prosecutor has not tendered into evidence and which are very important. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, it is disappointing that you were not able to absorb more quickly the essential nature of the documents, because your cross-examination this morning in respect of the date of wounding and discharge was on a quite misleading basis given that you had those documents before you, and even the first of them, the one-page document, ought to have made it evident that the foundation for your cross-examination was wrong. With respect to the document of which there is only one page and which is not complete, we notice that the witness says that the document is correct. I propose that we will receive it, noting it to be incomplete. If the balance of the document is not received, the weight we will be able to attach to the document will be very slight, if anything. But in the anticipation that the balance may be found, we will receive the document in an incomplete form today. If the court officer would give the documents the exhibit number, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P57. May I inform Your Honour that we have not received copies for the Trial Chamber and their legal staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the usher could collect those being proffered. The first document, I take it, is the discharge letter dated 12 December 1991. That's Exhibit P57, which appears to be the last document in the bundle that is being put forward. The second document is an incomplete, undated letter of the Dubrovnik medical centre.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The third letter is a letter of the Medicinski Centre of Dubrovnik, dated 13th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything further, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During cross-examination, Mr. Rodic cross-examined you about the fact that you had a status of an invalid of war. Now, I want to show you a two-page document. Can you just spend a moment familiarising yourself with that two-page document. Mr. Valjalo, you've read it and familiarised yourself with the document. Is it a decision of the Croatian authorities recognising your status as an invalid of the war, dated on the 22nd -- 24th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the witness being told exactly what the document says, the document my learned friend is reading does not contain the words "war invalid status," but "military war invalid status," which is very important for my cross-examination and the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only -- I -- I'm not in a better position than Mr. Rodic, obviously, to translate the document. Again, it's a document which we had faxed from the witness's home on the weekend to the Prosecution. It hasn't been translated yet. We've had a -- we've only had it read to us. So I can't take that point. Our understanding is that it is something different. I can have the interpreters read the relevant extracts to Your Honours. It's -- the document is pursuant to a declaration published in the Croatian government Gazette, and we have the government Gazette here, again not translated. So it may be the best course is for the witness to identify the document as his or not, have the interpreters read the relevant extracts to Your Honours and take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course with all of these exhibits, there will be provided an authenticated translation in due course, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As quickly as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, what can you tell the Trial Chamber about that document?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document granted me the status of a military war invalid because I was performing my work obligation in the Crisis Staff, and that is the basis on which I was granted this status. Otherwise, I was not a military person. I was not in uniform. And this document was produced after a review of my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- go on.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing is, the president of the Executive Board was also the president of the Crisis Staff, and it was members of the Crisis Staff, if they were wounded, who got this status. I don't know anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other civilians or people in your own position who received a similar declaration?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others who were wounded, but who were given the status of civilian invalids of the homeland war. Those who were in the Crisis Staff, if any of them were wounded, were granted the status of military war invalids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the -- were those in the Crisis Staff wounded, were they combatants or non-combatants?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't fight, the ones I know. I don't know who all the members of the Crisis Staff were, but they were all in civilian clothes. I don't know exactly where this Crisis Staff was located, but the president of the Executive Board was at the same time the president of the Crisis Staff. I never saw him put on a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this declaration entitle you to?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a misinterpretation. I apologise. The witness said just awhile ago, speaking about the president of the Crisis Staff, the president of the military Crisis Staff. Line 18, page 41. He said the "military Crisis Staff." Here it just says "Crisis Staff." So please bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could perhaps the interpreters tell us what was actually said. My learned colleague Ms. Somers says she heard wartime Crisis Staff, not military Crisis Staff. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it would be possible for the interpreter to indicate what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not recall, but the recording can be checked, sound recording can be checked at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If that could be done. We noticed your concerns, gentlemen, and we will find out what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Might I ask that the interpreters also to read onto the record portions of this two-page document which has been provided to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If they would be so kind as to do that we ware grateful. You said portions, Mr. Re. Could you indicate what portions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The portions -- the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "While receiving this pension, he may not receive for the same invalidity remuneration for physical harm under the regulations of the pension and invalidity insurance."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please read from the bottom -- sorry, from the second last paragraph on the first page where it says Obrazlozenje and the first paragraph over the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Grounds. The application for the granting of the status of a military war invalid of the Croatian war of defence was submitted by the above-named to this administration on the 18th of December, 1992. In the proceedings prior to the issuing of this decision, the following was established: "That according to the -- according to the extract from the birth register, Mato Valjalo was born on the 18th of May, 1948. "That according to the certificate on the circumstances of his wounding issued by the office for defence of the Dubrovnik municipality, class 810-03/92-16/102, number 2117-04-05-92-2 of the 18th of December, 1992, Mato Valjalo was mobilised as having a work obligation while performing the duty of driver for the Crisis Staff of -- of the SO Dubrovnik and, "That he happened to be -- that he happened to be on the road, on Stradun, and was seriously wounded in several places all over his body on the 6th of December, 1991. "That he is not a beneficiary of remuneration for physical damage under the relations of the pension insurance a certificate (issued by the pension fund of Dubrovnik, number 041/19 of the 18th of December, 1992.) "That according to his citizenship certificate, he is a citizen of Croatia. "That according to the certificate of the Ministry of the Interior, the Dubrovnik police administration number 511-03-01, number 1/833/1992, he has never been convicted. "That according to the adduced medical documentation, the above-named was treated at the Dubrovnik medical centre, the KBC medical centre in Rijeka and in Thalasotherapija Opatija. "That the medical commission in the first instance to -- for persons covered by the law of the protection of military and civilian war invalids in Split in their finding and opinion number 462/93 of the 11th of February, 1993, estimated the invalidity of the above-named as being 30 per cent permanently for the following reasons: State after explosive wounding in the area of the back of the neck, in the area of the right shoulder blade, in the area of the right thigh and shin with foreign bodies remaining, movement in the right knee reduced, T. 104.a., 20 per cent, and Article 4. "In view of all of the above and the facts found and on the basis -- and pursuant to the provisions of the above-named law, the above-named fulfils the conditions for the granting of the status of a military war invalid in the ninth group with 30 per cent invalidity permanently and the right to a personal invalid's pension and special bonus.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's as far as I want you to go for these purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I thank the interpreter on behalf of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that also be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P60.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I indicate to the Trial Chamber this, for the record, this document was likewise provided to my learned colleagues from the Defence before the cross-examination continued this morning. The Prosecution will tender -- will seek to tender an extract from the relevant government Gazette declaration, an explanation of the civilian military invalidity and so on. We will have that translated before we do tender it. And in any case, it's a public record. That completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that you stated awhile ago that my cross-examination was not well founded but I can hardly not point out that the introduction of these documents at this time, and in the way in which my learned friend and colleague has presented these documents and tendered them into evidence was a stalling tactic in connection with the opinion you gave in relation -- in relation to my cross-examination. But I must say that by tendering these documents into evidence and by emphasising portions of these documents as read by the interpreters, has been a waste of valuable time. The most essential portions of the documents were not read out, nor were they properly highlighted. Also, I must tell you that the last document that was read out was only tendered after I had told you that the Defence will be submitting two further documents. There is another essential document, the most important document, I dare say, on which the decision is founded, the decision to grant Mato Valjalo the status of a military war invalid. What I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, and this is something that the Prosecution has not offered or disclosed so far, the Defence will attempt to tender this document too, but I would like to be given a chance to point out the most important portions of this document in cooperation with the witness if I just may be granted a little more time. It is the document I'm talking about. This was given to us just immediately before our cross-examination began. These are essential documents, crucial documents related to precisely what I was trying to do during my cross-examination and to this witness's fundamental status, which of course is very important as one of the counts in the indictment against General Strugar is also the wounding of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you wish to have leave to further cross-examine in respect of the document that has been provided to you only this morning and which you had not had the time to study when you were completing your cross-examination a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we were given a set of documents containing about ten documents. I certainly didn't have time to go through them in detail during my cross-examination, but in relation to this last document, what I would like to point out is the following: I would like to work through three very important passages with the witness's help, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're saying you'd like now to put some further questions to the witness about this further document which has not been tendered to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I was only given this during the break, and that was the first opportunity I had to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the circumstances, you should have that leave to further cross-examine, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic just said he was only given a document during the break. We don't know what document he's referring to. We provided these documents to Mr. Rodic this morning before the cross-examination began, and it would appear from the record that Mr. Rodic was in fact cross-examining on the contents of the documents based upon the numerous questions he asked of Mr. Valjalo, questioning his status as a civilian during December 1991. It was fairly apparent to the Prosecution sitting here. Your Honours, of course, didn't have those documents, but Mr. Rodic must have been going through the documents based upon the wording of some of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, we're wasting far too much time on this. A document which you have not put before us but which you provided just before the hearing commenced this morning we are told has not been the subject of detailed exploration with the witness and which is material in the view of the Defence to its case. So I propose to allow Mr. Rodic to cross-examine briefly on this further document, whatever it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will try to make it as short as possible. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. P62, Exhibit P62, can that be shown to the witness, please. Further cross-examination by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have no P62 yet, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P60. I said 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, at the top of the page on the right-hand side there is a stamp. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above the stamp there is a handwritten remark "Review completed," and the date is the 15th of December, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please take that document and check if my reading is correct. Inside the circle of the stamp, the first circle, it says "Dubrovnik defence office"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second line inside the circle of the stamp, "Dubrovnik defence administration." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third layer -- line of the first stamp in capital letters, "Defence Ministry." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just above that "The Republic of Croatia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the left upper corner, at the beginning it says "The Republic of Croatia, Dubrovnik municipality," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next passage, "Secretariat for health, social care, work, veterans, and invalids. Veterans and invalids administration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we please skip these numbers now and move to the next passage. The first paragraph starts like this: "The veterans and invalids administration of Dubrovnik municipality, in processing a request by Mato Valjalo from Dubrovnik, to have the status of military war invalid granted to him,"

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's more in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm asking you is what's important. Is that what says?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the disposition and decision under the Roman numeral I. Can you please read out what it says under the Roman numeral I.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How far along are we?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Decision," and then the Roman I. Can you please read out what it says? "Mato (Ivo) Valjalo iz Dubrovnika...."

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mato, son of Ivo Valjalo from Dubrovnik, Prijeko 19, born on the 18th of May, 1948, is granted the status of military war invalid of the 9th group with 30 per cent invalidity as of the 1st of January, 1992, permanent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom of this same page where it says grounds or statement of reasons, can you see that? The last passage on the page speaks about the documents that were reviewed when making the decision. You have two items towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1. The last item on the page.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to avoid going through the whole document. So the last item. "According to evidence," can you please read that out to us?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the -- the process that the following has been ascertained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please just read out the last item if you can.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That according to the".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just go slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That according to the extract from the birth register, Mato Valjalo was born only the 18th of May, 1948."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the next one. That according to --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That according to evidence on the circumstances surrounding the wounding, with the Dubrovnik defence office, class --" should I read the number out too?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, everything, please.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "810-03/92-16/102, filing number 21," I think it says 1, "2117-04-05-92-2, dated the 18th of December, 1992. Mato Valjalo, a mobilised conscript assigned a war assignment while working as the driver of the SO Dubrovnik Crisis Staff was caught while travelling," --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you speed up a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "- on the Stradun, seriously wounded, receiving several wounds over his whole body. Date: The 6th of December, 1991."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Can you please have a look at the bottom of page 2. Does it say: "Please forward to Mato Valjalo, Dubrovnik, Prijeko 19." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 2, "Defence ministry, department for the protection of the victims of the homeland war in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer be requiring this document. Prior to being issued this decision, were you also given any sort of certificate such as the one we've just read? Did you also enclose this with your application to the commission when you requested to be granted the status of a war invalid, this certificate that was issued by the Dubrovnik municipality defence office, did you attach that to your application too?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now read to you the following to jog your memory. "Republic of Croatia, Dubrovnik Neretva county, plus and number are identical to the number of the decision which you will see from the balance of the document, it says, "Pursuant to Article 171 of the law on general legal procedure, and pursuant to a request from the defence administration of Dubrovnik municipality, the following certificate is hereby issued: This is to officially certificate that Mato Valjalo, the driver of the former municipal assembly of Dubrovnik, from the first day, that is from the 15th of September, 1991, pursuant to his work assignment, was assigned to work for the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik municipal Assembly." Next passage: "From the very first day of the attack of the enemy army against Dubrovnik, Mato Valjalo worked as the driver, and he was at the disposal of the Crisis Staff around the clock." The first sentence of the third passage on the same page: "During the worst attacks on Dubrovnik, Mato Valjalo drove members of the Crisis Staff, municipal officials, and top politicians of the Republic of Croatia to military missions. On the 6th of December, 1991, he was wounded on the Stradun when on a mission given to him by the Crisis Staff". The balance of the passage explains how you got to the hospital, but that's not important now. And please allow me to read the fourth passage of the certificate to you: "The certificate is issued to the above named so that he can be granted the rights that he's entitled to as a result of the armed attack on the Republic of Croatia and the law on the protection of military and civilian war invalids." Do you remember this certificate being issued to you?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do remember when it was issued to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enclose this certificate when the decision was issued to you by the administration for veterans and invalids?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have, but I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This certificate, did you at a later stage forward it to the OTP together with these medical documents that have been tendered into evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't remember?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness this document so that he can again confirm what I've just read out is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't mind if the Defence wishes to tender it. It may shorten the process. It was a document faxed to us on the weekend. I didn't tender it because it hasn't been translated and I'm a little bit unsure about the contents. That's the only reason. We certainly don't object to the shortcut if they just tender it and it can be translated later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will certainly be tendering this document into evidence because it happens to be the most reliable and important document as far as the cross-examination was concerned. Certainly it is true that this document or the other documents that have been tendered have not yet been translated into English. I thank the Trial Chamber for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please say something about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Can you tell us whether what I read out from the document was correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your reading was correct. This is a later document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the administration for invalids and veterans with this document?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent this document to the review commission because my status as an invalid was abolished, so I filed a complaint.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please try not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember that this was sent back to me later on because I had filed a complaint about my status as an invalid being abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pursuant to this same decision, do you still enjoy the status after war invalid?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any further re-examination, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Excuse me for just one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, may we thank you for your attendance, and you are now free to go back home. You may now leave the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness for the Prosecution is Mr. Per Hvalkof who will be taken by Mr. Weiner. If we can just take a moment to do some shifting. Thank you, appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be kind enough to take the affirmation which will be placed in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would read from the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'd like to tender notebooks with approximately 42 documents which we'll be using during this examination. I'll announce the numbers. We won't always be going in order, but we will try to go in order as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What are these documents exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These are ECMM documents. This gentleman here will testify that he was the Danish representative to the ECMM. He was a supervisor of the monitors, the supervisor of the monitors in Dubrovnik and will be talking about a lot of these documents as to the happenings in Dubrovnik, letters to and from the accused, all sorts of information that they were receiving, logs, diaries, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So this is a bundle of monitoring mission documents, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will be using all with the exception of document 2, which is the exact same as document 4. They just have two different ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. As a bundle they will be received and can be separately identified by the tab numbers allocated within each bundle as they're dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P61.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May I begin? Thank you. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name to the Court. My name is Per Hvalkof. Could you tell us your date of birth and how old you are?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: My date of birth is the 8th of September, 1936 so I am 67 years old now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I live on a farm in a rural area in the northern part of a small dot called Denmark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a university degree?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: No, I haven't. In my country the educational system is slightly different. I have a -- I have passed through teachers college. I have an education as an army officer, and I have partly a -- gone through the agriculture university in forestry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you passed through teachers college. Do you have a degree from teachers college?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, I have a degree from teachers college.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your employment status at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I am an old page pensioner retired from both my military and civilian life seven years ago, I'm a widower, and I look after my farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever serve in the Danish military?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I have belonged to the Danish military from the 10th of August, 1955 until I retired on the 30th of September, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank upon retirement.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your 40 plus years in military, did you serve on a full-time basis or as a reserve office he was?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Both. Long periods about 18 years full time and all the time served -- the Danish army is a mobilising army so I was doing all the rest of years serving at least one month a year, now and then two or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you weren't serving as a -- when you weren't serving in the military, what are you doing?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: In the early years I was studying. I've always got a farm pretty early, looking after that, and later on when I got my teacher's education I worked as a teacher and for the last many years as the vice-principal of a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you served in the military did you serve in any peacekeeping missions?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I served in several peacekeeping missions for a period nearly covering 12 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What countries or places did you serve?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: India, Pakistan, Iraq, Iran, Syria, Jordan, Israel, Egypt, Lebanon and ex-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were severing as a peacekeeper did you have the opportunity to work with any Yugoslavian people's army units?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, I did in 1961 I served in the Danish-Norwegian battalion in the Gaza Strip and among all the battalions there there was a Yugoslav battalion and, by the way, one officer there later on became the head of and my boss in Iraq. He was a general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were the Yugoslavian soldiers subject to the same standards and regulations as the other units in on peacekeeping missions?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. Of course they were. They -- we were under UN command and we were also serving under the same conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being under UN command, did they take orders from officers from other units?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, we all took our orders in a normal military way from the various battalions from the unit headquarters. It was called the United Nations Emergency Force Number 1, actually. So we were all having -- we were all under UN command -- command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise. My fault.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the discipline of those JNA troops that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, I didn't work close with them. I met them. I have been a guest at their unit, and they seem extremely qualified like all the other units from India, Brazil, Canada, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, or whatever. They were like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you sent to Croatia at some time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. I've -- I've been there twice, actually, but I was sent in -- appointed to go down there in September 1991, and due to the various problems in Croatia at the time, we were not asked to come, or I was not asked to come before 15th of October. I arrived in Zagreb as an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ECMM that you refer to? What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: European Commission Monitor -- sorry. I say again, the European Commission Monitor Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went to Zagreb in 1991, October 1991, were there any other Danish soldiers with you?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: We were not sent down as soldiers. We were sent down as civilians, and the majority of us were reserve officers or the other part were diplomats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hold any special position in relation to this delegation of Danish reserve officers and other civilians?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: It was called the Danish delegation, and I was appointed by the Minister of Foreign Affairs in Denmark as the head of this delegation. Other countries had ambassadors. In my case I happened to be a fancy major, and farmer, and teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb until the 23rd of October, and then I was appointed the deputy head of the new arranged so-called Regional Centre, Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to leaving Zagreb, did you receive any briefings?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had the opportunity first to read whatever files were available about the Dalmatian coast, covering the area there Karlobag down to Dubrovnik. That means south-east of Dubrovnik as far as the Croats were controlling the area, and I had a verbal briefing by one of the staff officers at the head ECMM headquarters. Sorry, I may correct a mistake I made before. I said the EC -- it was the EC community. I said something else before. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you say EC, so European Community Monitoring Mission, not the European Commission.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you went to Split, were you involved in establishing a Regional Centre there?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. When the head of mission was an Italian Ambassador or the head of Regional Centre Split was an Italian ambassador, and I was his deputy head of the Regional Centre. In my language, his second in command. And the job for a person like that is to arrange all the practical work, the staff work, make all the coordination and be the daily leader of how the organisation operates, and of course to replace the head of the centre when he was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did the operational centre or the Regional Centre in Split become operational?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: It became -- well, to be exact, we started operating from the very first day, we had only very few people, and some -- so we had to have the whole thing organised. That takes a bit of time. We had to find place to stay and to get organised. So it was in full operation with about altogether 60 people on the 28th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is a Regional Centre?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, when I came. The whole operation by the ECMM was organised and controlled from the headquarters in Zagreb, but they found out, which is anyway a good -- was very good idea in my experience and way of thinking, that it would be more good to have, for example, a centre down in Split operating on Dalmatian coast in order to be close to the people you were dealing with, in order to have people in the area getting in contact with the two opposing parties so you could get to know each other and they could -- you could have a feeling of confidence and trust which is always very important in peacekeeping missions. And the head of mission and the staff apparently found out that that was a good idea, and that's why they put us down there, and that was why we immediately after that - completely according to my way of thinking - placed people permanently in -- in -- for example, in Dubrovnik, we had a team there or two. Zadar, Sibenik, and they were the places we had people permanent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt the examination. Is this the break time, Your Honour, or should I continue for a while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can go for a little longer, Mr. Weiner, unless it's convenient for you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It makes no difference to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think a little longer. We were running a little late, and I would be happier getting a little further into the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what area was your Regional Centre responsible for?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: As I said before, the Dalmatian coast from the Karlobag and down to Dubrovnik, that means all area on the Dalmatian coast from Karlobag controlled by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there other Regional Centres in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know if they established other afterwards. I was pretty much busy and concentrated. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I'd like to talk about records. Were records prepared and kept by the ECMM personnel? Were they prepared and kept?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. It was working, let's say, as a -- as a normal peacekeeping operation for where you have UN military observers. That means, actually, in a very army type of way. So people reported. It might be during normal communication or it might be in writing, but anyway, it always ended up in writing when it was brought by radio, for example, or phone. And like in any staff, then you handle these matters and you file it and you forward whatever has to be forwarded to your higher headquarters. So we kept files, and in a normal filing system like any organisation like that would do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the normal course of your daily work, did you review, examine and consider these records and documents?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Every day we had of course our daily staff meetings. We had every day our daily debriefings. When the people we were sending up from our headquarters in Split came back, they reported, and we had -- we were all orientated at the daily debriefing. And when people came back from, let's say, Dubrovnik, Zadar, or Sibenik, they were sending regular reports, but when they came back they gave a debriefing of the whole period they had been away and that was normally about ten to 14 days. Differed a bit according to the situation and the requirement for people maybe having to go out to other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever use any of these documents in your decision-making?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Of course. That's why we had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the documents that you kept or maintained, were these prepared close in time to the events in which they discussed?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, they were. As soon as possible. In cases when you are standing out investigating or something in the field, you might take notes, but as soon as people could, you would go back, take notes, and write their debriefing report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were documents also kept in Zagreb at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, the -- whatever was important for Zagreb. Of course, some matters were of no value, but majority of whatever was reported to us was forwarded to the headquarters in just -- in the standard way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever examine the records in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Would you say that again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever examine any records in Zagreb in relation to Dubrovnik and Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: No, I did not. The only dock use I saw in Zagreb were the documents I mentioned before which I read before I went to Dubrovnik -- or, sorry, before I went to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having reviewed these documents, were you able to learn who was the commander of the JNA forces in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed and to the best of my knowledge I also read that General Strugar was the commander of the JNA in the Dubrovnik area. And that applied also later. Whatever information I got, it was the same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told we have only a few minutes left on the tape, so if that's a convenient time, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have our 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, I'd like to invite your attention to a document at tab 1, the first tab of the notebook. It's a letter dated October 19th, 1990. Is that a correct date?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. It should be.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Sorry, no. It's 1991. It couldn't be 1990. Somebody has scribbled in the wrong year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is that letter to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, it is to General Strugar, and it is -- there's no signature, but it's apparently from the ECMM team in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that the -- or did you know that the ECMM team in Dubrovnik had written or was involved in certain letters of protest --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- To General Strugar and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever seen any of these types of letters in Zagreb or Split, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also aware of any conflict occurring at that time around October 19th, October 20th between General Strugar and the ECMM team?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what seemed to be the problem? Sorry. What was the problem at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, there were apparently conflicts concerning -- I think it was something with the road and repair of the road, and there was a feeling apparent that -- that people found it was difficult to negotiate with the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the JNA side's view of the ECMM team in Dubrovnik at that time or on the -- October 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, according to what they told me, they found that it was not so pleasant to negotiate with the JNA, and they found it difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we'll come back to -- now, we'll come back to that first letter at tab 1. Could you please look at tabs 4, 5, 6, and 7, which are letters dated October 19th and 20th. Starting with tab 4. It's a letter dated October 19th. Who is that letter to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: It's for General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it from?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, again down at the bottom it's the ECMM team in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that, the request of that letter, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, the request of the letter from the ECMM team is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't remember these by heart, but I have to look for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the last line of the letter.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, the last line of the letter says: "We therefore again stress strongly that you have to withdraw behind your own lines."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- now, again also in the middle of the letter, if you look, it also says that "especially all armed forces should by all means not interfere with this process and withdraw behind their own lines." Was there a problem at the time involving parties not staying within their lines, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, as you know, this was made on the 19th of October, and I was still in Zagreb, but there was no doubt that their was a problem according to the information I had. And in general, it was -- seemed to be a problem all over that there -- whatever was promised was not kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it also says in the third full paragraph that "after 19 days of fighting the repairment -- after 19 days of fighting, the repairment of the road in the defensive position of the commune of Dubrovnik can only be regarded as an aggressive act contrary to the confidence you're appealing to in your message of 1740 hours." This aggressive act of repairing the roads, isn't that the same complaint in letter one that we saw in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we go to tab 5. That's dated October 20th at 1945 hours. Now, is this General Strugar's response?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: As far as I can see, yes, it is. And it is from General Strugar to the ECMM team, we've got the same abbreviation again, in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us about the tone of this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, I could say I don't like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence: "The arrogance of your mission being informed that the people of Dubrovnik have not invited the JNA does not contribute to the goodwill and objective," something, "of the problems -- objective scrutiny of the problems to be solved." Now, sir, is this a continuing part of the problem or tensions that the team was having at that time in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: As I said, I was not there at the time. I have not talked to these people who wrote this, none of them, but as I mentioned before, the monitors who had dealt with the JNA down in that area felt uncomfortable about the meetings they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence of this letter says: "The decision of the withdrawal of the JNA to a certain line will be brought by the relative authorities of Yugoslavia, and the JNA will obey those decisions consequently." What was your view of that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, you could say if it means that they would do something about withdrawing to the lines where they were supposed to be it would be all right, but I could add that they -- it might be a good idea to -- to have the neutral people sort of being present and confirming this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- was it unusual for the local commander to go to Belgrade or the national government for decisions?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I don't know how the Yugoslavian army was working, but in my opinion, a decision like that in an area like that should be taken by the local commander. It shouldn't be that difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look at the next letter, tab 6. Which was sent five minutes after General Strugar's letter. It's also October 20th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What worries me is the foundation for these documents that my learned friend and colleague has laid. These are not letters by this witness to anyone, nor are these letters that this witness ever received. I am not quite sure I understand the foundation for these documents to be introduced, why these letters are presented in this way and why this witness is being examined as to the contents of these letters based on quotes from the letters given that the witness is only reading the documents here and perhaps speculating about them. But this, I don't believe, is really an integral part of his testimony here. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's early. I'm taking these four letters together and then we're going to discuss them a bit, and then if they want to object that's fine, but I think it's premature at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question raised is the evidentiary foundation of documents of which this witness was not immediately an author and was not involved in their preparation and preceded his time in office, if I understand his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you assist the Chamber with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. Your Honour, documents here are admissible pursuant to 89(C) which says a Chamber may admit any evidence which it deems to have probative value. In Prosecutor versus Delalic which was consideration on the motion of the Prosecution for the admissibility of evidence which is dated 12 -- I'm sorry, 19 January 1998, states in paragraph 16: "The approach adopted by the Rules is clearly one in favour of admissibility as long as the evidence is relevant and is deemed to have probative value, and its probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." Similarly in Prosecutor versus Blaskic, which in the judgement on 3 March 2000 it says: "The principle embodied by the case law of the Trial Chamber on the issue is one of extensive admissibility of evidence. Questions of credibility and authenticity being determined according to weight given to each of the materials by the Judges at an appropriate time." Now, with regard to the issue of authenticity, we have several decisions in this Tribunal. The most recent is Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic on its orders on the standards governing the admission of evidence which is 15 February 2002. At paragraph 19 the Chamber notes that when objections are raised on the grounds of authenticity, the Trial Chamber will, and this is in quotes: "This Trial Chamber will follow the practice this Tribunal has previously adopted, namely to admit documents and video recordings and then decide what weight to give them in the context of the Trial Record." Further, there has never been a requirement at this Tribunal that a document's author must testify in order for it to be admitted, and that comes from Prosecutor versus Delalic, the same decision that I just mentioned, but in paragraph 22. As you can note, the Tribunal has tried to review as much evidence as it can. This Tribunal, the Nuremberg Tribunal, the Rwanda Tribunal. It takes as much evidence as it can but doesn't get into major evidentiary conflicts as to admissibility and authentication. Now, with regard to ECMM documents, I can state offhand that there have been three different courts that have had rulings or admitted these documents. Let us begin with the case of Prosecutor versus Tuta and Stela Tuta and Stela, which is commonly then as the Tuta and Stela case. Prosecutor versus Naletelic and Martinovic. And in that case they didn't have an ECMM official come in and present documents. They didn't have an ECMM official come in and discuss the documents. In that case, they had an investigator who went to ECMM and just seized records or took records and came in and said, "These are the records that I have." They had no evidence as to authenticity in that case. And there was a decision in that case on 31 January 2002, decision on the admission of ECMM documents, and in that case, if the Court goes to look, they admitted the documents. They had the same situation occur in that same case relating to international -- I'm -- international organisation documents and battalion documents from another peacekeeping monitor -- set of peacekeeping monitors. And in that situation, in another decision on 13 December 2001, they admitted those documents. In the Milosevic case, in the Croatian part of the Milosevic case through witness Colm Mangan, they introduced the documents while he was a member of the monitoring team. However, they also introduced documents -- one document of the monitoring team's log concerning weeks after he had left the area. In the Milosevic case in Bosnia, they had an ECMM employee come in, according to the chief Bosnian Prosecutor, who was not familiar with any of the documents, did not recall who wrote them. However, as an ECMM employee, he was allowed to introduce all of the ECMM documents, and they have been admitted in the Milosevic case. In the Kordic case, in the Kordic case not only did the Prosecution introduce ECMM documents, but the Defence complained that they didn't have access to the ECMM documents. And on 3 May 2000 in Prosecutor versus Kordic and Cerkez there was an ex parte application for an issuance of an order to the European Community Monitoring Mission asking them, or ordering them to give access to the Defence so they could see the documents, so they could tender the documents. In other cases, either ECMM documents, international documents, have been admitted. In the Samac case which is the Prosecutor versus Simic, Tadic, and Zaric, without a witness a Prosecutor stood up and introduced documents of the International Red Cross concerning exchanges which occurred in the area. The evidence relating to this area is overwhelming. When the issue is authenticity, the issue -- the matter goes to the weight and not the -- and not the issue of admissibility. Further, if I continue with this witness, I can continue to lay a foundation and you'll get more of an idea of his knowledge of these documents and his familiarity with these documents as well as the situation which occurred. Therefore, the Prosecution would state that it is overwhelming that these documents are relevant, they provide a context and background to the situation, and that they should be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Weiner, that the witness will be able to confirm that the documents that are here which appear to be dated before his time with the monitoring mission are documents of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. These are all documents of the ECMM. We've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will the witness be able to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. So far he's testified that these are ECMM documents, and I'll testify that he can seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has said that about the first document but none that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I haven't got to that. I have one more document. I've taken those four in a row and I haven't got to the rest of my questioning on that. If you allow me to proceed I can get to that part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just very briefly. I will not even try to be as extensive as my learned friend and colleague, but I will try to say two things. Firstly, our objection concerns the following: Mr. Weiner asked the witness to comment on a document that he did not write or send, nor did he receive it. He's asking for comments on documents. Your Honour, our objection was not about these documents being tendered into evidence. They may as well be tendered into evidence and accepted as such, as far as we are concerned, but how can the witness be in a position to interpret anything that is in any of these documents since he was not part of the mission at the time? How should he know what people thought or did at the time before he arrived. The essence is he doesn't know anything about the content of these documents. That's the essence of what I was trying to say. We have faced such situations before where documentary is accepted on the basis of submissions with no witnesses whatsoever. And then the Trial Chamber decides whether the exhibits will be accepted or not with no further testimony. Our point is this witness is not able to testify to what people did or thought just on the basis of pure speculation since he was not yet in the area at the time and had no direct knowledge of these documents. We accept that these documents will be accepted as exhibits, but we don't believe that the witness should be asked to talk about something that he has no direct knowledge of. By the way, may it also be said that all these documents cited by my colleague have already been tendered into evidence when the first witness Adrien Stringer testified. So all these have been tendered, the documents cited by my learned friend and colleague today. He may as well have a look, because when Mr. Stringer testified, he analysed these documents. I can't give you the exact numbers now, but it should be easy enough to compare the two lists and we are certain to do this during our cross-examination. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that last observation correct in your understanding, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. These four documents which are tabs 4, 5, 6, and 7 were all documents for identification, marked for identification and were not accepted as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There appears to be no question being as to the authenticity of the document and as to its origin, and you, Mr. Weiner, assure us that the witness will confirm these documents are ECMM documents. Their admissibility can, therefore, be accepted. You have not put any submission, Mr. Weiner, about the concern which Mr. Petrovic has now clarified about you seeking to have the witness comment on documents of which he has no personal knowledge, comment on the content of the document. Do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness, if he is allowed to testify further after we finish the documents, will tell us that he is aware of this situation. This was the situation that he walked into, that in the final document it says that the matter is being -- the matter of the complaints of General Strugar have been sent up the line to Zagreb because they felt it was that significant, that he learnt of these problems, that he knew the history of it, and coming into the situation he was aware of this and had seen some of these letters -- of these four letters here and was fully aware of the situation and had to deal with that when he came in and oversaw the next monitoring team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think you may on balance continue with your present line of questioning, Mr. Weiner, and we will hope that your hopes for the witness's evidence will be fulfilled. If not, we may have to revisit Mr. Petrovic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just very quickly look at tabs number 6 and then 7. The first one is tab 6. It's a document dated October 20, 1991. And can you tell us who it's from and who it was sent to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, it's from Captain Jeremic. I have had different titles for him but Captain Jeremic to the ECMM in Dubrovnik. I can add that I have seen these documents before, but as it was mentioned, I was not there. I cannot, of course, remember exactly what was written, but I had read them before -- read them before I was serving in Split, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with a Captain or a commander, Komandir Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: I had met him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I had dealings with him in Zelenika on the 12th of November, and I had dealings with him again before -- when we returned to Zelenika shortly, two days later, and I had dealings -- I met him at the meetings with Admiral Jokic on the 6th of December and on the 7th -- sorry, correction, on the 5th of December and on the 7th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you had dealings with him, who was he representing?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: He was representing the JNA, and he was also now and then called the liaison officer of the JNA and General Strugar's liaison officer. When my met him he was along with Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the next letter.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us who that's from?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: That's from the ECMM monitors in Dubrovnik, and it's addressed to Captain Jeremic, and it's an answer of the previous one as far as --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the end of that letter, if you go to the second page, sir, it says: "We ask you to inform General Strugar that we are consulting our headquarters in Zagreb in view of his message of today of 1945 hours. Since we are operating on behalf of the EEC Presidency in The Hague and the general expressed his doubts as to our neutrality, we feel it necessary to bring this matter up to our headquarters in Zagreb." Are questions of neutrality serious matters for monitors?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly is. You cannot operate as a neutral observer, monitor, call it whatever without being -- your neutrality is complete and there is no doubt about it. And it's for a -- for example, a United Nations military observer and in this case an EC monitor, it's a very serious allegation. I would never accept personally an allegation like that, and I have -- I -- fortunately, nobody has ever in my work done so to me. I consider it serious because you cannot fulfil and carry out your jobs if you're not neutral and you -- there must be absolute -- you must be able to prove for sure that the man is not neutral before you put in this allegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that you were aware of the situation that was going on, this conflict, this tension that was occurring.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, I was aware of it because as I mentioned, I had read those papers at the time. I was aware of it because when I met monitors who had served down in the Dubrovnik area, they were not feeling too happy about their relationship with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any ideas of what to do based on that situation when you arrive at Split, based on the tension or to ease the tension?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Well, the only way to ease the tension is then to try to communicate with the party the best way you can. You will have to -- the way you act to prove to people that you are a neutral person and you can be trusted. And, well, we briefed people about that. They were fully aware of the monitors, that they had to do their very best to gain the confidence of the people they dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you continue in October and turn to tab 3, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this type of document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes. I have read it before, but I cannot give you all the details of what is in it now but, yes, I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this considered an analysis-type document or --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: To me it is an analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know whether or not the Old City had been bombed in October or shelled in October of 1991, the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: The Old Town, no, I'm not sure, but it -- Dubrovnik was, to the best of my knowledge, whatever it was, the old part or new part, it was -- had received shells, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the third sentence in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The Old City is being bombarded. Yes. I have to admit I couldn't remember, but yes, it is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really, really must object to this. I would really like to know what's going on here. The witness clearly states he does not know what this document is. He can't remember, and yet my learned friend and colleague reads out a portion to him and he doesn't know whether it's the Old Town or the new town. Then he sees in the document that it's the Old Town and then his testimony suddenly is that the Old Town was shelled. I'm not sure this is an appropriate way to ask questions. If you look at the transcript you will see that he said he was not familiar with the document. He can't remember.
